sm: The host, John Donvan, opens this Open to Debate episode, recorded at Arizona PBS studios with Arizona State University's Institute of Politics. He chats with former senator Jeff Flake and the organization's chief executive about civil disagreement and why deepfakes matter. They note that about thirty states are grappling with laws on the topic. Donvan then tells of a fake video of the carrier Abraham Lincoln on fire that briefly alarmed President Trump. The question is whether AI-generated deepfakes should be treated as protected political speech, and he introduces the four debaters.

Donvan introduces the debaters. Robert Corn-Revere of FIRE and Nina Jankowicz, who once led a short-lived Homeland Security disinformation board, argue for the proposition. Susan Benesch of Harvard's Berkman Klein Center and Ryan Calo, a University of Washington law professor, argue against. He explains that the live audience votes before and after, and sets rules of civility. In his opening, Corn-Revere says all speech is presumptively protected, with only narrow unprotected categories like defamation and fraud. He argues that depicting things politicians never did is an old tradition, citing Franklin, Thomas Nast and South Park.

Corn-Revere adds that thirty-one states have restricted political deepfakes, but that regulating new technology first has a long history, and some of these laws have been enjoined by courts. Benesch opens for the con side with examples: fake videos of a Texas student accusing candidate James Talarico, and a fake candidate in Slovakia's election. She says deepfakes are harder to detect, labels do not work, and they spread fast. She also argues AI itself has no free speech rights. Jankowicz, herself a victim of deepfake abuse, says she opposes giving government power to regulate such speech, especially under an administration she says abuses it.

Jankowicz argues that content provenance watermarking, backed by more than six thousand companies, can help people tell real from fake, though it needs wider adoption and education. Calo says the First Amendment protects the marketplace of ideas, and deepfakes threaten that. He cites the fake Biden robocall in New Hampshire and the liar's dividend, where politicians dismiss real evidence as fake. He notes that the Supreme Court allows punishing false, harmful speech, citing the Alvarez case. Donvan summarizes that the pro side says dangers may be exaggerated, while the con side says deepfakes corrode shared reality.

The panel reacts to a labeled deepfake video of Senator Jon Ossoff. Jankowicz says the label gives people enough context. Benesch cites a study in which nearly seventy percent of people missed AI labels. Corn-Revere says Ossoff and Talarico both won comfortably, so voters can parse such ads, and warns that line-drawing between parody and fakes means endless litigation. Calo replies that line-drawing is normal in law, and that people are affected even by things they know are fake. They also discuss a harmful real ad involving Amy Acton's mother, which Benesch says differs from a deepfake because the words were genuine.

Jankowicz says that in 2024 and since, voters and reporters quickly spotted deepfakes and they did not sway outcomes. Benesch counters that winning margins do not show nobody was persuaded, and that a 2026 review of twenty-five studies found deepfakes erode trust in news. Corn-Revere doubts any major impact has been shown. They then consider the viral AI image of a girl with a puppy after Hurricane Helene. Corn-Revere says a real photo used the same way would have the same effect, so AI is not the issue. Calo notes such fakes may not fit defamation, since the people are not real.

Calo describes a fake in India about child kidnappers that led to lynchings, where no one could sue for defamation. Jankowicz suggests platform payments for viral content are a separate issue to fix. Benesch says AI fakes erode people's ability to tell truth from lies, and AI is moving faster than humans can adapt. Corn-Revere says unprotected categories like defamation still apply to AI. Calo says bribery shows harmful acts can be banned even if elections are unaffected. An audience member asks how impact can be measured, and Benesch agrees that election results are too narrow a metric.

Calo says courts allow banning speech that is both false and harmful, such as impersonating a government official, and that existing defamation and fraud laws are inadequate. Benesch argues that free speech is a human right, so AI has none. Jankowicz says a human always stands behind an AI agent. Corn-Revere warns that state laws can be viewpoint-based and let government favor one candidate, and Jankowicz points to Singapore. In closings, Jankowicz cites Russian activists jailed under speech laws and quotes Thomas Jefferson on educating the people. Calo cites 1,488 deepfake incidents in 2026, including a fake Josh Shapiro with an estimated 180 million views.

Calo closes by comparing deepfakes to the printing press and libel law, and urges a no vote. Corn-Revere says the bigger threat is letting politicians sue or prosecute over parody, citing President Trump's lawsuits, and that existing laws already cover crimes like the Biden robocall. Benesch replies that careful, narrow regulation would not cause an avalanche of litigation, and that Brandeis's counterspeech remedy was an untested guess. The audience vote before the debate was seven point seven percent yes, eighty-four point six no, and seven point seven undecided. Afterward it was sixteen point seven yes and seventy-five percent no, so the pro side won.
